titre: Michael Polanyi: We Know More Than We Can Tell
accroche: You spot a friend's face in a crowd of a thousand people in a split second. Try explaining how: you won't be able to.
contenu_vulgarise:
You spot a friend's face in a crowd of a thousand people, in a split second, without thinking. Now ask yourself what, in that face, let you recognize it among all the others: you will not be able to answer. You know how to recognize that face, but you do not know how to say how.

This observation, mundane yet hard to explain, is what the chemist turned philosopher Michael Polanyi (1891-1976) places at the center of his last major book, *The Tacit Dimension*, published in 1966 from lectures given at Yale. His now-famous formula fits in one sentence: “we can know more than we can tell.”

## The Mechanism

Polanyi distinguishes two ways of knowing. The first, called focal, concerns an object one looks at directly: the letters of a word, the muscles one tenses to keep balance on a bicycle. The second, called tacit, concerns the details one uses without noticing them in order to reach that object: one does not think about each muscle used while riding, and that is exactly why one rides without falling. Knowing how to ride a bicycle, Polanyi says, does not even require knowing the correct theory of balance: one can ride perfectly while holding a false idea of the physics involved.

Polanyi, who had a career as a chemist before turning to the philosophy of science in the 1930s, stands squarely against the positivism that then dominated: the idea that any knowledge worthy of the name could, in principle, be stated entirely in explicit rules, verifiable one by one. For him, this idea ignores the tacit foundation on which all explicit knowledge rests, including the most formalized scientific theories.

## What This Shifts

We often picture scientific knowledge as a set of rules one need only list and then apply, a manual that could, in theory, be fully handed down in writing. Polanyi shifts this picture: even the most rigorous researcher recognizes a pattern in data, judges that an experiment “looks” to be going wrong, or spots a badly set instrument at a glance, without always being able to justify that judgment by a rule statable in advance. That judgment is learned from a mentor, through repeated example, not only from a book.

His son, John Polanyi, a chemist like him, received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1986 for his work on the dynamics of elementary chemical reactions. The anecdote illustrates, in its own way, the father's point: the skill of a great chemist is never fully captured by what he can write in a paper.

citation.texte: We can know more than we can tell.

carte.punch: You recognize a face in a crowd of a thousand, but you cannot say how.
carte.idee: In 1966, chemist turned philosopher Michael Polanyi argued that we always know more than we can tell: riding a bicycle or recognizing a face draws on tacit knowledge, learned by example, that no written rule can fully replace.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Biography of John Polanyi, son of Michael Polanyi, 1986 Nobel laureate in Chemistry for his work on the dynamics of chemical reactions.

quiz.question: Why does Michael Polanyi choose the example of riding a bicycle to illustrate tacit knowledge?
choix: Because one can know how to ride a bicycle without knowing, or even correctly knowing, the physical theory of balance
Because learning to ride a bicycle objectively takes longer than learning a scientific theory
Because balance on a bicycle rests on an innate reflex, present from birth in every individual
Because the bicycle was, in the 1960s, the most common example used by philosophers of science
quiz.explication: Polanyi stresses this point: one can ride perfectly well while holding a false idea of the physics of balance, proof that the knowledge involved is not a set of rules one would state and then consciously apply, and not a matter of learning time, innate reflex, or academic fashion.
